pack.description: Cross-disciplinary academic vocabulary: the words used to describe research, argue a point and report evidence in any field.
pack.selection_note: Internal high-yield selection of words that recur across all academic subjects; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.

entries.example_spoken: The library restricts access to that room after nine.

entries.definition: to keep something or continue to have it
entries.example_academic: Clay soils retain water far longer than sandy ones.
entries.example_spoken: I read the chapter twice but retained almost nothing.

entries.definition: to use one thing or person in place of another
entries.example_academic: Producers substituted cheaper materials when prices rose.
entries.example_spoken: You can substitute yogurt for cream in this recipe.

entries.definition: based on general ideas rather than on real things or events
entries.example_academic: The discussion remained abstract and offered no practical recommendations.
entries.example_spoken: That's too abstract for me; can you give an example?

entries.definition: to gradually get more of something over time, or to increase gradually
entries.example_academic: Toxins accumulate in the bodies of animals at the top of the food chain.
entries.example_spoken: I've accumulated way too many open tabs.

entries.definition: next to or very near something
entries.example_academic: Samples were taken from the forest and from adjacent farmland.
entries.example_spoken: The parking lot is adjacent to the gym.

entries.definition: to officially give something, such as money or time, to a particular purpose or person
entries.example_academic: Only two percent of the budget was allocated to research.
entries.example_spoken: We allocated ten minutes to each speaker.

entries.definition: similar in some way to another thing, so that a comparison is useful
entries.example_academic: The wing of a bat is analogous to the human arm.
entries.example_spoken: It's analogous to learning to drive: awkward at first, then automatic.

entries.definition: to expect something and prepare for it
entries.example_academic: Planners failed to anticipate the growth in car ownership.
entries.example_spoken: I didn't anticipate so many questions after my talk.

entries.definition: not based on a reason, system or plan, and therefore seeming unfair or random
entries.example_academic: The boundary between the two categories is somewhat arbitrary.
entries.example_spoken: The word limit seems totally arbitrary.

entries.definition: to happen at the same time as something else, or to be the same
entries.example_academic: The rise in literacy coincided with the spread of cheap newspapers.
entries.example_spoken: My exam coincides with my sister's wedding.

entries.definition: to reduce the bad effect of something, or to pay someone for a loss
entries.example_academic: Higher yields compensated for the loss of farmland.
entries.example_spoken: Nothing can compensate for a bad night's sleep before an exam.

entries.definition: to combine well with something and make it more complete or effective
entries.example_academic: Field observations complement the data collected by satellite.
entries.example_spoken: The two courses complement each other really well.

entries.definition: to form an idea or plan in the mind; to imagine something
entries.example_academic: The canal was conceived as a way of bypassing the rapids.
entries.example_spoken: I can't conceive of doing all that in one week.

entries.definition: to keep someone or something within the limits of a particular place, activity or subject
entries.example_academic: The discussion is confined to the period before the reform.
entries.example_spoken: Please confine your comments to the topic.

entries.definition: to be different from what is usual or expected; to move away from a plan
entries.example_academic: Actual spending deviated sharply from the original estimate.
entries.example_spoken: He never deviates from his morning routine.

entries.definition: separate and clearly different from other things of the same kind
entries.example_academic: The process can be divided into four discrete stages.
entries.example_spoken: Think of it as three discrete tasks, not one big one.

entries.definition: to force something or someone out of its usual place, or to take its place
entries.example_academic: Factory production gradually displaced household weaving.
entries.example_spoken: The new dorm displaced the old tennis courts.

entries.definition: to change something so that it is no longer true or accurate, or no longer has its normal shape
entries.example_academic: Subsidies distort prices and encourage overproduction.
entries.example_spoken: The microphone distorts my voice.

entries.definition: including many different types of people or things
entries.example_academic: The reef supports an extraordinarily diverse community of fish.
entries.example_spoken: Our class is really diverse; there are students from twenty countries.

entries.definition: more important, powerful or noticeable than other things of the same type
entries.example_academic: Agriculture remained the dominant sector of the economy until the 1950s.
entries.example_spoken: English is the dominant language in the lab.

entries.definition: to include a large number or range of things
entries.example_academic: The term encompasses a wide variety of farming systems.
entries.example_spoken: The course encompasses everything from grammar to public speaking.

entries.definition: to involve something as a necessary part or result
entries.example_academic: Any expansion of the port would entail the loss of wetlands.
entries.example_spoken: What exactly does the internship entail?

entries.definition: stated clearly and exactly, leaving nothing to be guessed
entries.example_academic: The contract makes no explicit reference to overtime.
entries.example_spoken: The professor was explicit: no late submissions.

entries.definition: suggested or understood without being stated directly
entries.example_academic: There is an implicit assumption that all firms have equal access to credit.
entries.example_spoken: There was an implicit criticism in her question.

entries.definition: to include something as part of a larger whole
entries.example_academic: The revised model incorporates data on rainfall and soil type.
entries.example_spoken: I incorporated your comments into the second draft.

entries.definition: certain to happen and impossible to avoid
entries.example_academic: Given the scale of the debt, some form of default was inevitable.
entries.example_spoken: A few mistakes are inevitable when you speak fast.

entries.definition: to make something begin
entries.example_academic: The ministry initiated a review of safety procedures.
entries.example_spoken: She initiated the conversation, not me.

entries.definition: to become involved in a situation in order to change what happens
entries.example_academic: The central bank intervened to stabilize the currency.
entries.example_spoken: The resident advisor had to intervene in the argument.

entries.definition: fair, reasonable or allowed by law
entries.example_academic: Critics raised legitimate concerns about the reliability of the data.
entries.example_spoken: That's a legitimate question, and I don't have the answer.

entries.definition: seeming likely to be true or reasonable
entries.example_academic: A more plausible explanation is that the tools were traded, not made locally.
entries.example_spoken: His excuse sounded plausible, so I let it go.

entries.definition: happening before something more important, as a preparation or first stage
entries.example_academic: Preliminary results suggest that the treatment is safe.
entries.example_spoken: These are just preliminary ideas; nothing is decided.

entries.definition: very careful and thorough, with high standards
entries.example_academic: The drug underwent rigorous testing before it was approved.
entries.example_spoken: It's a rigorous program, so expect a lot of work.

entries.definition: to provide information that supports a statement or theory
entries.example_academic: Tree-ring data corroborate the written accounts of the drought.
entries.example_spoken: Can anyone corroborate your story?

entries.definition: to make something clear by explaining it more fully
entries.example_academic: The experiment helped to elucidate the role of the enzyme.
entries.example_spoken: Could you elucidate what you mean by "soon"?

entries.definition: to make a bad situation or problem worse
entries.example_academic: The drought exacerbated tensions between farmers and herders.
entries.example_spoken: Skipping meals will only exacerbate your headaches.

entries.definition: to make something less harmful, serious or painful
entries.example_academic: Planting trees along the river mitigated the effects of flooding.
entries.example_spoken: A good outline mitigates the risk of running out of time.

entries.definition: showing awareness of small but important differences in meaning or opinion
entries.example_academic: A more nuanced account recognizes that the reform had winners and losers.
entries.example_spoken: Her answer was more nuanced than a simple yes or no.

entries.definition: a typical pattern or model of something; a set of ideas that shapes how a subject is understood
entries.example_academic: The discovery overturned the dominant paradigm in the field.
entries.example_spoken: Remote work is a completely different paradigm.

entries.definition: to suggest that something is true as a starting point for reasoning
entries.example_academic: The theory postulates the existence of particles that have never been observed.
entries.example_spoken: He postulated that the noise came from the pipes.

entries.definition: to prevent something from happening or make it impossible
entries.example_academic: The poor condition of the bones precludes any firm conclusion about diet.
entries.example_spoken: A part-time job doesn't preclude you from applying.

entries.definition: to claim to be or do something, especially when this may not be true
entries.example_academic: The document purports to be a letter written by the king himself.
entries.example_spoken: The site purports to offer free textbooks, but it's a scam.

entries.definition: to prove that a statement or theory is wrong
entries.example_academic: Later experiments refuted the claim that the effect was universal.
entries.example_spoken: I couldn't refute his argument, even though I disliked it.

entries.definition: to provide evidence that proves something is true
entries.example_academic: The author fails to substantiate the claim with any figures.
entries.example_spoken: You need to substantiate that point with a source.

entries.definition: not certain or fixed, and likely to change later; done without confidence
entries.example_academic: The authors offer a tentative explanation that requires further testing.
entries.example_spoken: We have a tentative plan to meet on Thursday.

entries.definition: to support or form the basis of an argument, theory or system
entries.example_academic: Three assumptions underpin the model, and each can be questioned.
entries.example_spoken: Trust underpins every good study group.

entries.definition: completely clear and without any possibility of doubt
entries.example_academic: The evidence for human influence on the climate is unequivocal.
entries.example_spoken: Her answer was an unequivocal no.

entries.definition: so weak, slight or uncertain that it hardly exists
entries.example_academic: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pretty tenuous excuse for missing the meeting.

entries.definition: an opinion or idea formed without enough evidence; a guess
entries.example_academic: The origin of the manuscript remains a matter of conjecture.
entries.example_spoken: That's pure conjecture; we don't know why she left.

entries.definition: a division into two things that are presented as completely different or opposite
entries.example_academic: The dichotomy between nature and nurture is now regarded as misleading.
entries.example_spoken: It's a false dichotomy: you can work hard and still sleep.

entries.definition: to estimate something unknown by extending what is already known
entries.example_academic: It is risky to extrapolate from a single city to the whole country.
entries.example_spoken: You can't extrapolate from one bad quiz to the whole semester.

entries.definition: to put two things next to each other in order to show how they differ
entries.example_academic: The exhibition juxtaposes ancient pottery with contemporary sculpture.
entries.example_spoken: The article juxtaposes two students' very different experiences.

entries.definition: according to what is stated or appears to be true, though the real situation may be different
entries.example_academic: The tax was ostensibly temporary, yet it remained in force for forty years.
entries.example_spoken: He came ostensibly to return a book, but he stayed two hours.

entries.definition: directly related to the matter being considered
entries.example_academic: The committee asked several pertinent questions about funding.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pertinent point; let's add it to the slides.

entries.definition: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way
entries.example_academic: Younger investors show a greater propensity to take risks.
entries.example_spoken: He has a propensity to volunteer for everything.

entries.definition: false or not genuine, although seeming to be real or true
entries.example_academic: The apparent link between the two variables turned out to be spurious.
entries.example_spoken: That's a spurious argument, and you know it.

entries.definition: more than is needed or wanted; unnecessary
entries.example_academic: The final chapter is largely superfluous and repeats earlier arguments.
entries.example_spoken: Cut the superfluous words and your email will be clearer.

entries.definition: to describe or mark something precisely, especially its limits
entries.example_academic: The report delineates the responsibilities of each agency.
entries.example_spoken: We should delineate who does what before we start.

entries.definition: to give a false impression of something, or to show that a belief about it is wrong
entries.example_academic: The calm tone of the report belies the scale of the financial losses it describes.
entries.example_spoken: His relaxed smile belied how nervous he actually was before the interview.
entries.example_interview: My grandmother's quiet manner really belies how much she has achieved; she ran a business for forty years.
entries.example_discussion: Sam's figures look reassuring, but they belie a deeper problem: the gains are concentrated in two cities.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "give a false impression of" — not "contradict" in the sense of arguing. French speakers sometimes use it as "nier", which is deny.

entries.definition: to draw attention to something and show that it is important
entries.example_academic: The latest outbreak underscores the need for faster testing in rural clinics.
entries.example_spoken: That near miss really underscores how careful we have to be in the lab.
entries.example_interview: That experience really underscored for me how much a good mentor can change things.
entries.example_discussion: The professor's example underscores a point Lena only hinted at: access matters more than cost.
entries.usage_note: Formal, common in academic writing. Same meaning as "underline"; never "souligner" in the sense of drawing a line under text.

entries.definition: to show that a claim, theory or suspicion is correct
entries.example_academic: Later excavations bear out the hypothesis that the site was occupied all year round.
entries.example_spoken: The numbers bear out what you said in the meeting.
entries.example_interview: I always thought early starts made me more productive, and my grades this year have borne that out.
entries.example_discussion: The survey data bear out Daniel's claim, at least for students who live on campus.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Usually "the data/results bear out a claim". The object can come between the parts: "bear this out". Irregular: bore, borne.

entries.definition: to make an argument, a position or a feeling stronger by adding support
entries.example_academic: Additional interviews would bolster the claim that the policy changed public attitudes.
entries.example_spoken: A couple of strong references could really bolster your application.
entries.example_interview: Working in the lab bolstered my confidence more than any class did.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's second example bolsters her argument, because it comes from a completely different country.
entries.usage_note: Neutral to formal. Takes an argument, case, confidence or position as object. Do not confuse with "boost", which is about amounts.

entries.definition: to make a statement, feeling or effect less extreme by balancing it with something else
entries.example_academic: The authors temper their optimism by noting that the sample came from a single region.
entries.example_spoken: I'd temper that conclusion a bit, because we only asked twelve people.
entries.example_interview: I'm excited about the internship, but I try to temper my expectations until I know the team.
entries.example_discussion: I agree with Marco, but I would temper his conclusion: the study only covered one season.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Temper a claim / expectations / enthusiasm" = make it less extreme. French "tempérer" exists, but learners rarely use the English verb.

entries.definition: to understand something difficult or mysterious after thinking about it carefully
entries.example_academic: Early naturalists could not fathom how such fragile insects crossed entire oceans.
entries.example_spoken: I can't fathom why they scheduled the exam on a holiday.
entries.example_interview: I honestly couldn't fathom why my roommate wanted to live without a fridge.
entries.example_discussion: It is hard to fathom how the policy could succeed without any funding for teachers.
entries.usage_note: Mostly negative or with "hard to": "I can't fathom why…". It means understand, not "sonder" in the sense of polling.

entries.definition: to deliberately avoid using or doing something
entries.example_academic: The author eschews technical jargon so that general readers can follow the argument.
entries.example_spoken: She eschews social media completely during exam season.
entries.example_interview: I've always eschewed group chats for project work; I'd rather meet in person.
entries.example_discussion: The authors deliberately eschew technical terms, which is why I found the article persuasive.
entries.usage_note: Formal and literary. Pronounced /ɪsˈtʃuː/. In speech, "avoid" or "steer clear of" is more natural.

entries.definition: to remove a difficulty or make an action unnecessary
entries.example_academic: A shared database would obviate the need for each lab to repeat the same measurements.
entries.example_spoken: Booking online obviates the need to queue at the office.
entries.example_interview: Having all my notes online obviates the need to carry folders around campus.
entries.example_discussion: Online forms would obviate the need for students to queue, as Kim points out.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Almost always "obviate the need for/to". It does not mean "obvious"; French speakers sometimes link the two.

entries.definition: to put forward an idea as a basis for argument or reasoning
entries.example_academic: The model posits a direct link between childhood diet and adult height.
entries.example_spoken: You're positing that everyone reads the instructions, which nobody does.
entries.example_interview: In my thesis I posit that small towns adapt faster than cities, which surprised my supervisor.
entries.example_discussion: Ana posits a direct link between screen time and sleep, but her sources only show a correlation.
entries.usage_note: Formal, academic. "Posit that…" or "posit a link/the existence of". Not "poser" in the general sense of putting something down.

entries.definition: to treat two distinct ideas or things as if they were the same
entries.example_academic: Public debate often conflates correlation with cause, which distorts the evidence.
entries.example_spoken: You're conflating being busy with being productive.
entries.example_interview: People often conflate being busy with being productive, and I used to make that mistake too.
entries.example_discussion: I think Jonah conflates two different issues: whether the policy works and whether it is fair.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Structure: "conflate X with/and Y". Useful in discussions to point out a confusion politely.

entries.definition: to make progress or movement slower or more difficult
entries.example_academic: A shortage of reliable data hampered early efforts to model the epidemic.
entries.example_spoken: The rain really hampered our plans for the field trip.
entries.example_interview: My lack of Spanish really hampered me during my first month abroad.
entries.example_discussion: Poor public transport hampers any effort to reduce car use in rural areas.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Takes progress, efforts or people as object. Close to "hinder"; "hamper" is also a noun (a basket), unrelated.

entries.definition: to have a negative effect on something, often by limiting it
entries.example_academic: New surveillance rules may impinge on the privacy of ordinary users.
entries.example_spoken: I don't want my job to impinge on my study time.
entries.example_interview: I don't let my part-time job impinge on my study time; I keep weekends separate.
entries.example_discussion: Monitoring student emails would impinge on their privacy, whatever the intention.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Always "impinge on/upon". French speakers often say "impinge something" without the preposition.

entries.definition: to put something valuable at risk of being harmed or lost
entries.example_academic: Delays in funding could jeopardize the entire ten-year study.
entries.example_spoken: Missing another deadline could jeopardize your scholarship.
entries.example_interview: I didn't want to jeopardize my scholarship, so I dropped one of my extra activities.
entries.example_discussion: Cutting the research budget now could jeopardize projects that took years to set up.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Spelled "jeopardise" in British English. Object: safety, future, chances, a project.

entries.definition: to be greater or more important than something else
entries.example_academic: For most patients, the benefits of the treatment clearly outweigh the risks.
entries.example_spoken: Honestly, the cost outweighs the convenience for me.
entries.example_interview: For me, the benefits of living on campus clearly outweigh the cost.
entries.example_discussion: Even if the program is expensive, its long-term benefits outweigh the initial investment.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, very useful in Academic Discussion: "the benefits outweigh the costs". No preposition after it: not "outweigh on" or "outweigh over".

entries.definition: to describe something as larger, more important or more certain than it is
entries.example_academic: Early reports overstated the effect, which later studies found to be modest.
entries.example_spoken: I think you're overstating how hard the course is.
entries.example_interview: I think people overstate how hard it is to learn a third language once you have two.
entries.example_discussion: Kim overstates the case: the evidence shows a modest effect, not a revolution.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Overstate the case / the importance". Opposite: "understate". Avoid "over-exaggerate", which is redundant.

entries.definition: to make something seem less important or serious than it really is
entries.example_academic: The company downplayed the safety concerns raised by its own engineers.
entries.example_spoken: Don't downplay your role in the project; you did most of the work.
entries.example_interview: I tend to downplay my own role in group projects, which my professor told me to stop doing.
entries.example_discussion: The report downplays the cost of maintenance, which is where most projects fail.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Same meaning as "play down". Object: risks, importance, role. Not "minimize" in the mathematical sense.

entries.definition: to explain something complicated, or to start to fail and fall apart
entries.example_academic: Geneticists are still trying to unravel how the two traits interact.
entries.example_spoken: The whole plan unraveled once the main speaker cancelled.
entries.example_interview: It took me a whole semester to unravel how the university's credit system actually works.
entries.example_discussion: Unraveling the causes of the decline requires data from several decades, not one survey.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Two senses: explain something complex, or fall apart ("the plan unraveled"). Spelled "unravelled" in British English.

entries.definition: to make an action or belief seem reasonable or necessary
entries.example_academic: The preliminary results warrant a larger trial with a more varied sample.
entries.example_spoken: A small scratch hardly warrants a trip to the emergency room.
entries.example_interview: A small delay doesn't warrant a complaint, in my opinion; things happen.
entries.example_discussion: The evidence does not warrant such a strong conclusion, so I would phrase it more cautiously.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means "justify". Often negative: "hardly warrants". French speakers sometimes confuse it with "guarantee" (warranty).

entries.definition: to make it difficult for something to happen or develop
entries.example_academic: High transport costs hindered the spread of the new farming methods.
entries.example_spoken: Too much caffeine can actually hinder your concentration.
entries.example_interview: Being too much of a perfectionist sometimes hinders me more than it helps.
entries.example_discussion: Strict visa rules hinder the exchange of researchers, as Paolo's example shows.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: progress, development, people. Pronounced /ˈhɪndər/, short i.

entries.definition: to reduce or limit something, especially an activity or a right
entries.example_academic: The new regulations curtail the use of pesticides near rivers.
entries.example_spoken: We had to curtail the trip because of the storm.
entries.example_interview: I had to curtail my social life a bit during exam season, which was hard.
entries.example_discussion: If governments curtail funding for public libraries, students from poorer families lose the most.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means reduce or limit. Object: spending, rights, activities. Not used for physically cutting something.

entries.definition: to prevent something from happening by acting before it can occur
entries.example_academic: The government lowered interest rates to forestall a recession.
entries.example_spoken: I emailed the professor early to forestall any confusion about the deadline.
entries.example_interview: I always confirm meeting times in writing to forestall any confusion.
entries.example_discussion: Clear rules on data sharing would forestall many of the disputes Mia describes.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means act early to prevent. Less common than "prevent", so it stands out in a written answer.

entries.definition: to make information or results inaccurate by giving them a particular bias
entries.example_academic: Because only volunteers were surveyed, the sample may skew the results toward enthusiasts.
entries.example_spoken: One really high score can skew the class average.
entries.example_interview: My first impression of the city was skewed by the terrible weather that week.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's survey only reached students in the library, which may skew the results.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Skew the results/data"; the adjective "skewed" is very common. Pronounced /skjuː/.

entries.definition: to judge or measure something, such as a feeling or an amount, when it is not obvious
entries.example_academic: The survey was designed to gauge public support for the new transport plan.
entries.example_spoken: It's hard to gauge how the professor feels about my draft.
entries.example_interview: In interviews, I try to gauge the mood of the room before I make a joke.
entries.example_discussion: It is difficult to gauge public opinion from social media alone, since most users never post.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Spelled g-a-u-g-e, pronounced /ɡeɪdʒ/. French speakers often misspell it "guage".

entries.definition: to gather or obtain support, attention or information
entries.example_academic: The proposal garnered support from both farmers and environmental groups.
entries.example_spoken: Her video garnered thousands of views in a single day.
entries.example_interview: Our student project garnered more attention than we expected, including a local newspaper article.
entries.example_discussion: The proposal has garnered support from both teachers and parents, which makes it more realistic.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Object: support, attention, praise, votes. In speech, "get" or "attract" is more natural.

entries.definition: to be a perfect example of a quality or type of thing
entries.example_academic: The cathedral epitomizes the ambitions of the late medieval city.
entries.example_spoken: That café epitomizes everything I love about this neighborhood.
entries.example_interview: For me, my old neighborhood epitomizes what a community should feel like.
entries.example_discussion: The new library epitomizes the shift Ana mentions: from storing books to hosting people.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Noun: "epitome" /ɪˈpɪtəmi/, four syllables. Means "be a perfect example of", not "summarize".

entries.definition: to express the main features of something in a short, clear form
entries.example_academic: The final chapter encapsulates the author's argument in a few memorable pages.
entries.example_spoken: That one sentence really encapsulates what the course is about.
entries.example_interview: One phrase from my grandfather encapsulates his whole philosophy: work hard, then rest properly.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's last sentence encapsulates the dilemma: we want innovation but fear its costs.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means capture the essence in a short form. Useful to introduce a summary in Academic Discussion.

entries.definition: to suggest or indicate in advance that something will happen
entries.example_academic: The minor protests of 1847 foreshadowed the upheavals of the following year.
entries.example_spoken: The first episode kind of foreshadows the ending, if you pay attention.
entries.example_interview: Looking back, my first summer job foreshadowed the career I want now.
entries.example_discussion: The protests of the 1960s foreshadowed many of the debates we are having today.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Mostly about events or stories. Do not use it for weather forecasts ("forecast").

entries.definition: to make a doubt, fear or false belief disappear
entries.example_academic: The new evidence should dispel any doubt about the origin of the samples.
entries.example_spoken: Talking to the tutor helped dispel my worries about the exam.
entries.example_interview: My first week here completely dispelled my fear that I wouldn't make friends.
entries.example_discussion: Better data could dispel the myth that young people do not care about local politics.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: myth, doubts, fears, rumors. Spelled with one l in "dispel", two in "dispelled".

entries.definition: to show that a popular idea or belief is false
entries.example_academic: Several studies have debunked the claim that we use only ten percent of the brain.
entries.example_spoken: That video completely debunks the rumor about the parking fees.
entries.example_interview: I love videos that debunk popular myths about nutrition.
entries.example_discussion: Several studies have debunked the idea that multitasking makes people more efficient.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, slightly informal. Object: myth, claim, theory. Stronger than "question": it shows the idea is false.

entries.definition: to avoid stating something too firmly, for example by adding limits or conditions
entries.example_academic: Careful writers hedge their claims when the evidence comes from a single study.
entries.example_spoken: He kept hedging and never really answered the question.
entries.example_interview: When I'm not sure of an answer in an interview, I hedge a little instead of guessing wildly.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah hedges his claim carefully, which I think makes it more convincing, not less.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Hedge a claim" = make it less absolute. Also "hedge one's bets". Useful vocabulary for talking about writing itself.

entries.definition: to add limits or conditions to a statement so that it is less general
entries.example_academic: The authors qualify their conclusion by noting that the effect disappears in older adults.
entries.example_spoken: Let me qualify what I said earlier: it's true for most students, not all.
entries.example_interview: I'd qualify what I said earlier: online classes work well for me, but only for theory.
entries.example_discussion: I agree with Sara, though I would qualify her point: the effect depends on the age group.
entries.usage_note: Formal in this sense. "Qualify a statement" = add limits. French speakers mostly know only "qualify for" (se qualifier).

entries.definition: to begin talking about a difficult or sensitive subject
entries.example_academic: The report broaches the question of whether the museum should return the objects.
entries.example_spoken: I wasn't sure how to broach the subject of rent with my roommate.
entries.example_interview: During my internship, I had to broach the topic of unpaid overtime with my supervisor.
entries.example_discussion: Few speakers broach the question of who will maintain the new parks once they are built.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Almost always "broach the subject/topic/question". Pronounced /broʊtʃ/, like "brooch".

entries.definition: to mention something indirectly instead of naming it clearly
entries.example_academic: The poem alludes to a famous shipwreck without ever naming the vessel.
entries.example_spoken: She alluded to some problems at home but didn't go into detail.
entries.example_interview: My professor alluded to a surprise in the final exam, which made everyone nervous.
entries.example_discussion: Kim alludes to the cost of the program but never says who would pay for it.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Always "allude to". Noun: "allusion". It means mention indirectly, not "make allusion".

entries.definition: to help a feeling, an idea or a skill develop over time
entries.example_academic: Small seminars foster the kind of debate that large lectures rarely allow.
entries.example_spoken: The club really fosters a sense of community among international students.
entries.example_interview: Team sports fostered a sense of discipline in me that I still rely on.
entries.example_discussion: Group projects foster cooperation, but only when roles are clearly defined.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: debate, cooperation, a sense of… Also means caring for a child temporarily ("foster parents").

entries.definition: to encourage an activity or development, or make it happen faster
entries.example_academic: Falling prices spurred the adoption of solar panels in rural areas.
entries.example_spoken: Seeing my friends graduate spurred me to finish my thesis.
entries.example_interview: Failing my first exam actually spurred me to change my study habits.
entries.example_discussion: Lower prices could spur demand for electric cars, but only if charging stations follow.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Spur someone to do something" or "spur growth/innovation". Past: "spurred", double r.

entries.definition: to make something happen sooner or more quickly
entries.example_academic: The drought hastened the decline of an already weakened empire.
entries.example_spoken: Stress can hasten the onset of a cold.
entries.example_interview: Moving abroad hastened my independence; I had to learn to cook within a week.
entries.example_discussion: Cutting maintenance budgets will only hasten the decline of public transport.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Pronounced /ˈheɪsən/, silent t. Object: decline, end, process. Not used for people hurrying in modern speech.

entries.definition: to make a problem or a difficult situation worse
entries.example_academic: Poor communication compounded the effects of the initial engineering error.
entries.example_spoken: Skipping breakfast only compounds the problem.
entries.example_interview: I missed the bus, and the rain compounded the problem, so I arrived soaked.
entries.example_discussion: Low wages compound the housing crisis, because workers cannot afford to live near their jobs.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. As a verb, stress on the second syllable: /kəmˈpaʊnd/. Means "make worse", not "compose".

entries.definition: to balance one effect with another so that the overall result does not change much
entries.example_academic: Gains in efficiency were offset by a sharp rise in demand.
entries.example_spoken: The cheaper rent offsets the longer commute.
entries.example_interview: The longer commute is offset by much cheaper rent, so I'm happy with my choice.
entries.example_discussion: The environmental cost of building the line would be offset within a decade by fewer car trips.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Past form is also "offset". Structure: "X is offset by Y". Useful for weighing pros and cons.

entries.definition: to reduce or stop the effect of something by producing an opposite effect
entries.example_academic: The drug counteracts the side effects of the earlier treatment.
entries.example_spoken: I drink a lot of water to counteract the dry air in the dorm.
entries.example_interview: I try to counteract long days at my desk with a walk every evening.
entries.example_discussion: Free tutoring could counteract some of the disadvantages Mia describes for rural students.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: effects, trends. Different from "counterattack". French "contrecarrer" is the closest equivalent.

entries.definition: to fit together well with something else, so that the two support each other
entries.example_academic: The archaeological findings dovetail neatly with the written sources.
entries.example_spoken: My internship hours dovetail nicely with my class schedule.
entries.example_interview: My part-time job dovetails nicely with my studies because it's in the same field.
entries.example_discussion: This proposal dovetails with Daniel's point about local control, so the two could be combined.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Dovetail with something" = fit together well. A woodworking metaphor; French speakers rarely know it.

entries.definition: to consider or judge something in a particular way, especially officially
entries.example_academic: Results were deemed significant only if they were confirmed in a second sample.
entries.example_spoken: The committee deemed my request reasonable, luckily.
entries.example_interview: My parents deemed it too dangerous for me to travel alone at sixteen.
entries.example_discussion: If a policy is deemed unfair by most citizens, it will not last, however efficient it is.
entries.usage_note: Formal, often passive: "be deemed necessary". French speakers tend to overuse "consider", which is fine but less precise.

entries.definition: to find out the truth about something by checking carefully
entries.example_academic: Investigators were unable to ascertain the exact cause of the collapse.
entries.example_spoken: Can you ascertain whether the library is open on Sunday?
entries.example_interview: Before choosing my major, I tried to ascertain what jobs graduates actually got.
entries.example_discussion: It is difficult to ascertain the long-term effects of the program after only two years.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Pronounced /ˌæsərˈteɪn/, stress on the last syllable. Means find out for sure, not "assert".

entries.definition: to guess or conclude something from the limited information available
entries.example_academic: Historians surmise that the letters were destroyed during the war.
entries.example_spoken: I surmised from her tone that the meeting hadn't gone well.
entries.example_interview: From his silence, I surmised that my friend hadn't enjoyed the film.
entries.example_discussion: One can only surmise why the author omitted the results from the second region.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Means guess from limited evidence. Stress on the second syllable. Not common in casual speech.

entries.definition: to state firmly that something is true, especially in an argument
entries.example_academic: Critics contend that the index overstates the real growth in wages.
entries.example_spoken: My roommate contends that pineapple belongs on pizza.
entries.example_interview: I would contend that the best teachers are the ones who admit when they are wrong.
entries.example_discussion: Marco contends that taxes are the only solution, but subsidies have worked elsewhere.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Contend that…" = argue firmly. Also "contend with" = deal with a difficulty, a different meaning.

entries.definition: to stop something from developing or being expressed
entries.example_academic: Excessive regulation can stifle innovation among small firms.
entries.example_spoken: I had to stifle a laugh during the presentation.
entries.example_interview: Too many rules can stifle creativity; that's what I noticed in my first job.
entries.example_discussion: Strict uniform policies may stifle self-expression, which is exactly Lena's concern.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: creativity, innovation, debate. Also "stifle a yawn/laugh". Pronounced /ˈstaɪfəl/.

entries.definition: to examine something very carefully to find details or problems
entries.example_academic: Reviewers scrutinized the statistical methods before the paper was accepted.
entries.example_spoken: My landlord scrutinized every scratch on the wall before returning the deposit.
entries.example_interview: Before I sign a lease, I scrutinize every line, ever since a bad experience last year.
entries.example_discussion: Any claim about health benefits should be scrutinized before it shapes school policy.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Noun: "scrutiny", often "under scrutiny". Spelled "scrutinise" in British English.

entries.definition: to support an argument or a system by giving it extra strength
entries.example_academic: The author buttresses her argument with data from three separate archives.
entries.example_spoken: You need more examples to buttress your point.
entries.example_interview: I buttressed my scholarship application with letters from two former employers.
entries.example_discussion: Kim buttresses her position with data from three countries, which makes it hard to dismiss.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Literally a support built against a wall. Object: argument, claim, case.

entries.definition: to obtain a reaction, an answer or information from someone
entries.example_academic: The questions were worded to elicit detailed answers rather than yes or no.
entries.example_spoken: My joke didn't elicit much of a reaction.
entries.example_interview: My question to the panel elicited a long silence, which was a little embarrassing.
entries.example_discussion: Open-ended questions elicit more honest answers than multiple-choice surveys.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Elicit a response/information". Do not confuse with "illicit" (illegal); they sound alike.

entries.definition: to make something seem less good, valuable or impressive
entries.example_academic: The minor errors do not detract from the overall value of the study.
entries.example_spoken: The noisy room detracted from an otherwise great talk.
entries.example_interview: The noise outside didn't detract from how much I enjoyed the concert.
entries.example_discussion: A few weak examples do not detract from the overall strength of Daniel's argument.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Always "detract from". Useful for concessive evaluation: "X does not detract from Y".

entries.definition: far greater than is reasonable or expected
entries.example_academic: The approval process takes an inordinate amount of time for small projects.
entries.example_spoken: I spent an inordinate amount of money on textbooks this term.

entries.definition: clear, logical and convincing
entries.example_academic: The essay presents a cogent case for reforming the funding model.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pretty cogent argument; I hadn't thought of it that way.

entries.definition: weak and not convincing, especially as evidence or as an excuse
entries.example_academic: The case rested on flimsy evidence from a single witness.
entries.example_spoken: That's a pretty flimsy excuse for missing the presentation.

entries.definition: likely to cause disagreement or argument
entries.example_academic: Funding for the project remains a contentious issue among council members.
entries.example_spoken: Let's avoid contentious topics at dinner with my parents.

entries.definition: present or noticeable in every part of something
entries.example_academic: The study documents the pervasive influence of advertising on children's diets.
entries.example_spoken: There's a pervasive feeling on campus that housing is too expensive.

entries.definition: happening in small steps, each adding a little to what came before
entries.example_academic: Most scientific progress is incremental rather than revolutionary.
entries.example_spoken: We made incremental changes to the app after each round of feedback.

entries.definition: matching something in size, amount or level
entries.example_academic: Salaries should be commensurate with experience and responsibility.
entries.example_spoken: The workload isn't commensurate with the credits we get for this course.

entries.definition: depending on something else happening or being true
entries.example_academic: Further funding is contingent on the results of the pilot phase.
entries.example_spoken: My summer plans are contingent on getting that internship.

entries.definition: almost the same in effect or seriousness as something worse
entries.example_academic: Ignoring the warning signs would be tantamount to accepting the risk.
entries.example_spoken: Skipping the final is tantamount to failing the course.

entries.definition: similar to something in character or quality
entries.example_academic: The process is akin to translation, since meaning must survive a change of form.
entries.example_spoken: Moving abroad felt akin to starting school all over again.

entries.definition: creating conditions that make something likely or possible
entries.example_academic: Open-plan offices are not always conducive to sustained concentration.
entries.example_spoken: My bedroom isn't exactly conducive to studying.

entries.definition: causing harm or damage
entries.example_academic: Chronic sleep loss has a detrimental effect on memory consolidation.
entries.example_spoken: Cramming the night before can be detrimental to your grades.

entries.definition: just beginning to develop
entries.example_academic: The nascent industry depended heavily on government contracts.
entries.example_spoken: Our nascent book club has exactly four members.

entries.definition: difficult to find, achieve, define or remember
entries.example_academic: A precise definition of intelligence has proved elusive.
entries.example_spoken: Sleep has been pretty elusive this week.

entries.definition: very difficult to solve, manage or control
entries.example_academic: Urban congestion has become an intractable problem for planners.
entries.example_spoken: The printer issue seems totally intractable.

entries.definition: done quickly, without attention to detail
entries.example_academic: A cursory reading of the data suggests a trend that closer analysis does not confirm.
entries.example_spoken: I only gave the article a cursory glance before class.

entries.definition: revealing something important, often something that was not meant to be shown
entries.example_academic: It is telling that none of the officials agreed to be interviewed.
entries.example_spoken: The silence after his question was pretty telling.

entries.definition: not justified by the facts or the situation
entries.example_academic: The study found that public fears about the vaccine were unwarranted.
entries.example_spoken: Honestly, the criticism of the team captain was unwarranted.

entries.definition: very unlikely to be true, and difficult to believe
entries.example_academic: The idea that the monument was built in a single season seems far-fetched.
entries.example_spoken: It sounds far-fetched, but I actually met the author on the train.

entries.definition: including or influencing every part of something
entries.example_academic: The overarching aim of the program is to reduce inequality in access to care.
entries.example_spoken: What's the overarching theme of your presentation?

entries.definition: done gradually and in small separate parts rather than with an overall plan
entries.example_academic: Piecemeal reforms have failed to address the structural causes of the shortage.
entries.example_spoken: The renovations have been really piecemeal, one room a year.

entries.definition: relevant to a subject being discussed
entries.example_academic: The committee asked that comments be germane to the proposal under review.
entries.example_spoken: That story is funny but not really germane to the question.

entries.definition: very important and influential on later work in a field
entries.example_academic: Her seminal paper on memory shaped two decades of later research.
entries.example_spoken: That album is kind of seminal for the whole genre.

entries.definition: too simple and not showing careful thought
entries.example_academic: The report offers a facile explanation for a deeply complex problem.
entries.example_spoken: Blaming the students is a pretty facile answer.

false_friend_fr.correct: en anglais, « facile » signifie « simpliste » ; « facile » au sens de « pas difficile » se dit easy

entries.definition: so complicated that it is difficult to follow
entries.example_academic: The original regulation was so convoluted that few farmers understood it.
entries.example_spoken: The instructions were way too convoluted; I gave up halfway.

entries.definition: until now or until the particular time being discussed
entries.example_academic: The archive contains letters that were hitherto unknown to historians.
entries.example_spoken: It's a hitherto unexplored part of the campus, at least for me.

entries.definition: as a result of the action that has just been mentioned
entries.example_academic: The city raised fares, thereby reducing the number of daily passengers.
entries.example_spoken: He skipped the review session, thereby missing the main hints.

entries.definition: directly and without trying to avoid something
entries.example_academic: The report places the blame squarely on poor maintenance.
entries.example_spoken: She looked me squarely in the eye and said no.

entries.definition: in a way that is clear and easy to notice
entries.example_academic: Survival rates improved markedly after the new protocol was introduced.
entries.example_spoken: The second draft is markedly better than the first.

entries.definition: used to introduce an idea that is the opposite of the one just mentioned
entries.example_academic: Higher temperatures speed up the reaction; conversely, cooling slows it down.
entries.example_spoken: Some students love group work; conversely, others find it exhausting.
entries.example_interview: When I'm well rested I learn fast; conversely, when I'm tired, nothing sticks.
entries.example_discussion: Higher fares might reduce crowding; conversely, they could push people back into their cars.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Introduces the reverse case. Not a synonym of "on the contrary", which corrects a statement.

entries.definition: to argue that a claim or criticism is false, giving reasons
entries.example_academic: The authors rebut the main objection by showing that the effect persists in older adults.
entries.example_spoken: She calmly rebutted every point he made during the debate.
entries.example_interview: In debate club I learned to rebut an argument without attacking the person who made it.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's point can be rebutted quite simply: the cheaper option has already failed twice.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Noun: "rebuttal". Close to "refute", but "rebut" stresses giving a counterargument rather than proving falsity.

entries.definition: to show that someone or something was right, after doubt or criticism
entries.example_academic: Later excavations vindicated the archaeologist's controversial dating of the site.
entries.example_spoken: The final results completely vindicated her decision to change the design.
entries.example_interview: When I got the scholarship, I felt vindicated, because everyone had told me not to apply.
entries.example_discussion: If the pilot program succeeds, it will vindicate Mia's view that small incentives can change habits.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Often passive: "feel/be vindicated". Not related to "revendiquer" (claim), a frequent confusion.

entries.definition: to support or strengthen something that is weak or likely to fail
entries.example_academic: The government borrowed heavily to shore up the struggling banks.
entries.example_spoken: We need a few more examples to shore up our argument.
entries.example_interview: Before my interview, I shored up my weak points by practicing with a friend.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel tries to shore up his case with one survey, but a single source is not enough.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Object: support, confidence, an argument, an institution. The object can come between the parts: "shore it up".

entries.definition: to find or separate information or meaning that is not obvious, with care and effort
entries.example_academic: The study teases out the separate effects of income and education.
entries.example_spoken: It took us an hour to tease out what the client really wanted.
entries.example_interview: Talking to my tutor helped me tease out what I actually wanted from my degree.
entries.example_discussion: It is worth teasing out two separate questions in Lena's post: cost and fairness.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, academic. Implies patient analysis. Not "tease" in the sense of joking with someone.

entries.definition: to be relevant to something or to affect it
entries.example_academic: These findings bear directly on the debate about class size.
entries.example_spoken: I'm not sure how that story bears on our decision.
entries.example_interview: My experience in retail bears directly on this job, because I dealt with customers every day.
entries.example_discussion: The study Ana cites does not really bear on our question, since it concerns adults.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "bear upon". "Have a bearing on" is a common equivalent. Not "bear" in the sense of tolerate.

entries.definition: to be relevant to a subject, or to deal with it, especially as evidence
entries.example_academic: The new data speak to a long-standing question about migration routes.
entries.example_spoken: Her record speaks to her commitment to the team.
entries.example_interview: I think my volunteering speaks to how much I care about education.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's example speaks to a broader problem: rules that are never enforced.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. In this sense it means "be evidence of" or "address", not "talk to someone". Very natural in American English.

entries.definition: to consider the advantages and disadvantages of something carefully before deciding
entries.example_academic: Policymakers must weigh up the costs of intervention against the risks of doing nothing.
entries.example_spoken: I'm still weighing up whether to take the job.
collocations: weigh up the pros and cons
entries.example_interview: I spent weeks weighing up the two offers before I chose this university.
entries.example_discussion: We need to weigh up the short-term cost against the long-term savings Mia describes.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, more British. American English often says "weigh" alone: "weigh the options".

entries.definition: to support a principle or decision and keep it in force
entries.example_academic: The court upheld the original ruling despite the new evidence.
entries.example_spoken: Teachers are expected to uphold the school's code of conduct.
entries.example_interview: As team captain, I had to uphold the rules even when my friends broke them.
entries.example_discussion: Schools should uphold the principle of equal access, whatever the cost.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Irregular: upheld. Typical objects: a decision, a ruling, the law, a principle, values.

entries.definition: to treat an idea or possibility as unimportant or not worth considering
entries.translation_fr: écarter, ne pas tenir compte de
entries.example_academic: We cannot discount the possibility that the samples were contaminated.
entries.example_spoken: Don't discount her advice just because she's younger than you.
entries.example_interview: I wouldn't discount the idea of working abroad later, even if I'm staying here for now.
entries.example_discussion: We should not discount Jonah's concern about privacy simply because it is hard to measure.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. As a verb meaning "dismiss", stress on the second syllable. French speakers mostly know only the noun (a price reduction).

entries.definition: to add more details to an idea, plan or argument
entries.example_academic: The second chapter fleshes out the theory with three detailed case studies.
entries.example_spoken: Can you flesh out your proposal before the meeting?
entries.example_interview: In my first job, my manager taught me to flesh out an idea before presenting it.
entries.example_discussion: Mia's proposal is promising, but it needs to be fleshed out with a budget.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. The object can come between the parts: "flesh it out". French speakers tend to say "develop", which is correct but vaguer.

entries.definition: to identify or describe something exactly, or to make someone give a clear answer
entries.example_academic: The exact cause of the decline is difficult to pin down.
entries.example_spoken: I tried to pin him down to a date, but he wouldn't commit.
entries.example_interview: It's hard to pin down exactly when I decided to study economics.
entries.example_discussion: It is difficult to pin down what Jonah means by "success", which weakens his argument.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Hard to pin down" is very common. With a person: "pin someone down" = force a clear answer.

entries.definition: to warn someone about a possible danger or problem, or to advise them to be careful
entries.example_academic: The authors caution that the sample was drawn from a single region.
entries.example_spoken: My tutor cautioned me against taking five courses at once.
entries.example_interview: My first manager cautioned me never to promise a deadline I couldn't keep, and I still follow that advice.
entries.example_discussion: Mia rightly cautions that a small pilot may not tell us much about a whole city.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Caution someone against + -ing" or "caution that…". As a reporting verb it is more precise than "say" or "warn".

entries.definition: to say something carefully or with some hesitation because it may be wrong or unwelcome
entries.example_academic: One reviewer ventured that the results might reflect seasonal effects.
entries.example_spoken: May I venture a guess about why the meeting was cancelled?
entries.example_interview: When my boss asked for ideas, I ventured that we could try a four-day week in summer.
entries.example_discussion: I would venture that both students underestimate how much teachers already do.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Venture an opinion / a guess", "venture that…". Signals modesty. Not "aventurer", which is not used this way.

entries.definition: to advise someone very strongly to do something
entries.example_academic: The committee urged the government to act before the winter.
entries.example_spoken: My friends urged me to apply, even though I had doubts.
entries.example_interview: My parents urged me to study abroad, and I'm glad I listened.
entries.example_discussion: Kim urges the school to act now, but she does not say where the money would come from.
entries.usage_note: Neutral to formal. "Urge someone to do" or "urge that someone (should) do". Stronger than "advise".

entries.definition: to decide that an idea or opinion is not important or not worth considering
entries.example_academic: Early critics dismissed the theory as speculation.
entries.example_spoken: She dismissed my worries with a laugh.
entries.example_interview: At first I dismissed coding as boring, but a summer course changed my mind.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel dismisses the cost argument too quickly, in my view.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Dismiss something as + adjective/noun". Also means "fire someone" or "let a class go", so context matters.

entries.definition: to describe someone or something with a word or phrase, often unfairly
entries.example_academic: The press labelled the policy a failure before any data were available.
entries.example_spoken: People label me shy, but I just like listening.
entries.example_interview: At school I was labelled the quiet one, but debate club changed that.
entries.example_discussion: Labelling the program a success seems premature when only one year of data exists.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Label X (as) Y". British spelling "labelled", American "labeled". Often suggests the description is unfair.

entries.definition: to give someone or something a name, often a humorous or descriptive one
entries.example_academic: Journalists dubbed the period the "lost decade".
entries.example_spoken: My friends dubbed me "the planner" because I organize everything.
entries.example_interview: My classmates dubbed our study group "the night shift" because we always met after ten.
entries.example_discussion: What Jonah dubs a "crisis" looks to me more like a slow, predictable decline.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, journalistic. Often passive: "be dubbed X". Also means "add a translated soundtrack" (doubler), a different sense.

entries.definition: to express sadness or disappointment about something
entries.example_academic: The author laments the loss of public spaces in modern cities.
entries.example_spoken: My grandfather often laments that nobody writes letters anymore.
entries.example_interview: I sometimes lament how little time I have for music since starting university.
entries.example_discussion: Mia laments the decline of local shops, but she does not explain how the plan would revive them.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Lament something" or "lament that…". Typical in reviews and essays to report regret about a loss or decline.

entries.definition: to criticize something strongly and publicly
entries.example_academic: Many economists decried the tax as unfair to small firms.
entries.example_spoken: Students decried the new parking fees at the meeting.
entries.example_interview: I've always decried the way some companies treat interns as free labor.
entries.example_discussion: Kim decries screen time in schools, yet her own example relies on an online platform.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Stronger than "criticize". Pronounced /dɪˈkraɪ/. Common in the press: "widely decried".

entries.definition: to praise something very enthusiastically
entries.example_academic: The report extols the benefits of early language learning.
entries.example_spoken: My aunt never stops extolling the virtues of her new diet.
entries.example_interview: My coach always extolled the value of rest days, which I ignored until I got injured.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel extols the program's flexibility but says little about its cost.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Usually "extol the virtues/benefits of". British spelling "extoll" is rare. Past: "extolled".

entries.definition: to praise someone or something publicly
entries.example_academic: The initiative was lauded by teachers and parents alike.
entries.example_spoken: Everyone lauded her for staying calm.
entries.example_interview: Our project was lauded by the jury, which was a huge surprise for the team.
entries.example_discussion: The policy has been widely lauded, yet the figures Mia cites suggest modest results.
entries.usage_note: Formal, often passive in the press: "be widely lauded". The adjective "laudable" (praiseworthy) is common.

entries.definition: to praise someone or something formally, often in public
entries.example_academic: The inspectors commended the hospital for its rapid response.
entries.example_spoken: My manager commended me on the report.
entries.example_interview: My supervisor commended me for handling an angry customer calmly.
entries.example_discussion: I commend Jonah for proposing a concrete budget, which is rare in this discussion.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Commend someone for/on something". Not "recommend", which is a different verb.

entries.definition: to state publicly that you support a person, idea or product
entries.example_academic: Several medical associations have endorsed the new guidelines.
entries.example_spoken: I'd endorse that plan if it were cheaper.
entries.example_interview: Our student union endorsed my proposal for longer library hours, which really helped.
entries.example_discussion: I fully endorse Kim's suggestion, with one reservation about timing.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Also "endorse a candidate/product". French "endosser" usually means taking on a role or a responsibility, so it is only a partial equivalent.

entries.definition: to repeat or express the same idea as someone else
entries.translation_fr: reprendre, abonder dans le sens de
entries.example_academic: The second report echoes many of the concerns raised in the first.
entries.example_spoken: I'd echo what Sam said about the deadlines.
entries.example_interview: I'd echo what my teachers always said: reading widely is the best preparation.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's point echoes the professor's question about who benefits most.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Very useful in Academic Discussion: "I would echo X's point that…". Past: "echoed".

entries.definition: to tell someone about something that happened, usually something you experienced
entries.example_academic: In her memoir, she recounts her first years as a researcher.
entries.example_spoken: He recounted the whole trip in great detail.
entries.example_interview: My grandmother loves to recount how she crossed the Alps on foot.
entries.example_discussion: The article Daniel cites recounts one family's story, which is not enough to generalize.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Stress on the second syllable. Different from "re-count" (count again), stressed on the first.

entries.definition: to describe the main facts or ideas of something without giving details
entries.translation_fr: exposer dans les grandes lignes, présenter
entries.example_academic: The first chapter outlines the main arguments of the book.
entries.example_spoken: Can you outline your plan in two minutes?
entries.example_interview: In my last job, I outlined a new filing system, and my team adopted it.
entries.example_discussion: Mia outlines three options, but only the second seems affordable.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Very useful to introduce a summary. Also a noun ("an outline").

entries.definition: to give more details or information about something
entries.example_academic: The authors do not elaborate on how the participants were selected.
entries.example_spoken: Could you elaborate a bit on that?
entries.example_interview: If you'd like me to elaborate on my internship, I can describe a typical day.
entries.example_discussion: I would ask Kim to elaborate on how the scheme would be funded.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Verb: /ɪˈlæbəreɪt/ + "on". French "élaborer" means "devise", a false friend: in English it means "give more detail".

entries.definition: to say something short and clever or funny
entries.example_academic: "Economics is common sense made difficult," the lecturer quipped.
entries.example_spoken: When I fell off the chair, my friend quipped that I'd finally found my level.
entries.example_interview: When I said I'd study abroad, my father quipped that he'd finally get the remote to himself.
entries.example_discussion: As one commentator quipped, the reform changes everything except the results.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Usually reports a witty remark. Past: "quipped".

entries.definition: to say something in a thoughtful way, as if thinking aloud
entries.example_academic: "Perhaps the question itself is wrong," the author muses in the final chapter.
entries.example_spoken: I sometimes muse about what I'd do if I won the lottery.
entries.example_interview: I often muse about how different my life would be if I'd stayed in my hometown.
entries.example_discussion: Lena muses on whether exams are necessary at all, which is a refreshing question.
entries.usage_note: Formal, literary. "Muse about/on/over". Reports a reflective remark, not a firm claim.

entries.definition: to suggest something indirectly instead of saying it clearly
entries.example_academic: The minister intimated that further cuts were likely.
entries.example_spoken: She intimated that she might leave the company.
entries.example_interview: My manager intimated that a promotion was possible, so I stayed another year.
entries.example_discussion: Daniel intimates that the teachers oppose the plan, but he gives no evidence.
entries.usage_note: Formal. The verb is /ˈɪntəmeɪt/; the adjective "intimate" (close) is /ˈɪntəmət/. Two different words.

entries.definition: to claim something, often falsely, or to state a belief openly
entries.example_academic: Many voters profess concern for the environment but drive to work alone.
entries.example_spoken: He professes to love cooking, but I've never seen him cook.
entries.example_interview: I don't profess to be an expert, but I've organized several events.
entries.example_discussion: Many schools profess a commitment to equity while charging high fees.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Often suggests the claim may be insincere: "profess to be". "Professer" in French means teach, a different sense.

entries.definition: to state firmly that something is true
entries.example_academic: The authors assert that the decline began earlier than previously thought.
entries.example_spoken: She asserted that she had never seen the email.
entries.example_interview: In meetings, I've learned to assert my ideas without interrupting others.
entries.example_discussion: Kim asserts that fines work, but the evidence from other cities is mixed.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Assert that…" = state firmly. "Assert yourself" = behave confidently.

entries.definition: to say that something is not true or not correct
entries.example_academic: Few historians dispute the date of the treaty.
entries.example_spoken: I don't dispute that the food is good; it's just expensive.
entries.example_interview: Nobody in my family disputes that my sister is the best cook.
entries.example_discussion: I do not dispute Mia's figures, only the conclusion she draws from them.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Dispute that…" or "dispute a claim". French "se disputer" (argue) is a different meaning.

entries.definition: to express doubt about whether something is correct, or ask a question about it
entries.example_academic: Reviewers queried the method used to measure stress levels.
entries.example_spoken: I queried a charge on my phone bill.
entries.example_interview: When I queried my final grade, the professor showed me exactly where I'd lost points.
entries.example_discussion: I would query whether the survey reached students who live off campus.
entries.usage_note: Formal, more British. "Query a figure/decision" = question it politely.

entries.definition: to say that you believe someone is honest or that something is true, from your own knowledge
entries.example_academic: Several colleagues were willing to vouch for her integrity.
entries.example_spoken: I can vouch for the café; the coffee is excellent.
entries.example_interview: My former manager can vouch for my reliability; I never missed a shift.
entries.example_discussion: I can vouch for the program Kim mentions, since my sister took it last year.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Always "vouch for". Common in references: "I can personally vouch for…".

entries.definition: to state an idea clearly, especially as part of an argument
entries.example_academic: The author makes the point that cheap energy has hidden costs.
entries.example_spoken: You made the point that we need more time, and I agree.
entries.example_interview: My coach always made the point that rest is part of training.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah makes the point that fees deter poorer students, and I think he is right.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Very useful to report someone's argument in Academic Discussion. Not "do the point".

entries.definition: different from what common sense would suggest, and therefore surprising
entries.example_academic: It seems counterintuitive, but adding a road can increase traffic.
entries.example_spoken: It's counterintuitive, but I study better with music on.
entries.example_interview: It sounds counterintuitive, but taking breaks made me finish my thesis faster.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's finding is counterintuitive: cheaper tickets led to fewer passengers.
entries.usage_note: Neutral, very useful to introduce a surprising result. One word in American English; "counter-intuitive" in some British texts.

entries.definition: not certain to be true, correct or honest, so open to doubt
entries.example_academic: The study's conclusions rest on a questionable assumption about income.
entries.example_spoken: Eating pizza for breakfast is a questionable choice.
entries.example_interview: Looking back, some of my first-year decisions were questionable, but I learned from them.
entries.example_discussion: The claim that grades improved is questionable, since the test itself was changed.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Polite way to express doubt. Also used about honesty ("questionable practices").

entries.definition: probably not true, honest or good; also feeling doubt
entries.example_academic: The company made dubious claims about the health benefits of its product.
entries.example_spoken: I was a bit dubious about the plan at first.
entries.example_interview: I was dubious about online classes, but they suited my schedule well.
entries.example_discussion: The statistics Jonah quotes come from a dubious source with an obvious interest.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Two senses: "a dubious claim" (unreliable) and "be dubious about" (feel doubt).

entries.definition: not based on facts or good reasons
entries.example_academic: Fears that the vaccine causes infertility proved ill-founded.
entries.example_spoken: Her worries about the move were ill-founded.
entries.example_interview: My fear of public speaking turned out to be ill-founded once I started practicing.
entries.example_discussion: I think Daniel's concern about costs is ill-founded, given the savings described in the report.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Common with "fears", "claims", "assumptions". Opposite: "well-founded".

entries.definition: based on good evidence or sound reasoning
entries.example_academic: There are well-founded concerns about the safety of the old bridge.
entries.example_spoken: Your doubts about the landlord were well-founded.
entries.example_interview: My parents' worry about the cost of living abroad was well-founded, as I discovered.
entries.example_discussion: Mia's skepticism is well-founded: similar schemes have failed elsewhere.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Often "well-founded fears/concerns". Hyphenated before a noun.

entries.definition: showing only one point of view; unfair
entries.example_academic: The documentary gives a one-sided account of the conflict.
entries.example_spoken: That was a pretty one-sided argument.
entries.example_interview: I try to read news from different sources so I don't get a one-sided picture.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's post is somewhat one-sided, since it ignores the views of teachers.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also "a one-sided match" (one team much stronger). Not "unilateral" in this sense.

entries.definition: fair and treating everyone equally
entries.example_academic: The report offers an even-handed assessment of both proposals.
entries.example_spoken: Our coach was always even-handed with the players.
entries.example_interview: As team captain, I tried to be even-handed when choosing who played.
entries.example_discussion: Lena's post is admirably even-handed: she weighs both options before deciding.
entries.usage_note: Formal. A precise compliment in a discussion post. Opposite: "one-sided".

entries.definition: showing a deep and accurate understanding of a person or situation
entries.example_academic: The essay offers an insightful analysis of rural poverty.
entries.example_spoken: That was a really insightful comment.
entries.example_interview: My most insightful teacher taught me to question my first answer.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah makes an insightful point about how schedules affect working students.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Good way to acknowledge a classmate before adding your view. Stress on the first syllable.

entries.definition: making people think seriously about something
entries.example_academic: The exhibition raises thought-provoking questions about memory.
entries.example_spoken: It was a thought-provoking film.
entries.example_interview: The most thought-provoking class I took was on the history of science.
entries.example_discussion: The professor's question is thought-provoking, because both answers seem reasonable.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Not the same as "provocative", which suggests deliberate offense.

entries.definition: new and very important, changing the way things are done
entries.example_academic: Her groundbreaking research changed how the disease is treated.
entries.example_spoken: The app was pretty groundbreaking when it came out.
entries.example_interview: I'd love to work on groundbreaking projects, even if they're risky.
entries.example_discussion: Calling the program groundbreaking seems excessive; similar schemes existed decades ago.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often overused in marketing; in academic writing, keep it for truly new work.

entries.definition: able to judge what will be needed in the future and plan for it
entries.example_academic: The city's far-sighted planners reserved land for parks a century ago.
