entries.example_spoken: It was far-sighted of you to book early.
entries.example_interview: My parents were far-sighted enough to start saving for my studies when I was born.
entries.example_discussion: Investing in rail now would be far-sighted, even if the benefits come later.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Opposite: "short-sighted". In American English, also means "hypermetropic" (eyesight).

entries.definition: not thinking about the future effects of an action
entries.example_academic: Cutting research funding would be short-sighted.
entries.example_spoken: It was short-sighted of me not to save any money.
entries.example_interview: Spending my whole first paycheck was short-sighted, and I learned my lesson.
entries.example_discussion: Closing rural libraries to save money seems short-sighted, as Mia argues.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also literal (myopic) in British English. Useful to criticize a policy politely.

entries.definition: based on wrong ideas or poor judgement, often despite good intentions
entries.example_academic: The campaign, though well meant, was misguided.
entries.example_spoken: I think the plan is a bit misguided.
entries.example_interview: My first business idea was well-intentioned but misguided, because I never checked the market.
entries.example_discussion: A total ban on phones strikes me as misguided, since many students use them for learning.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often paired with good intentions: "well-meaning but misguided". Softer than "stupid".

entries.definition: giving a wrong idea or impression
entries.example_academic: The graph is misleading because the scale starts at fifty.
entries.example_spoken: The ad was really misleading.
entries.example_interview: The job description was a bit misleading; there was far more admin than expected.
entries.example_discussion: Comparing the two cities is misleading, because their populations differ greatly.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Does not always mean deliberate lying. Verb: "mislead", past "misled".

entries.definition: made to seem larger or more important than it really is
entries.example_academic: Fears about the new technology turned out to be overblown.
entries.example_spoken: The hype around that restaurant is overblown.
entries.example_interview: My fear of moving abroad was overblown; I settled in within a month.
entries.example_discussion: Concerns about cheating in online exams seem somewhat overblown, given the data.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often "overblown fears/claims/rhetoric". Common in journalism and opinion pieces.

entries.definition: based on good reasoning or reliable evidence
entries.example_academic: The proposal rests on sound economic principles.
entries.example_spoken: That sounds like sound advice.
entries.example_interview: My father always gave me sound advice about money.
entries.example_discussion: Jonah's reasoning is sound, but his data come from a very small survey.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Sound reasoning/judgement/evidence". Not related to the noun "sound" (noise).

entries.definition: so carefully made or argued that no fault can be found in it
entries.example_academic: The prosecution's case appeared watertight.
entries.example_spoken: My excuse wasn't exactly watertight.
entries.example_interview: I try to make my reports watertight by checking every figure twice.
entries.example_discussion: Kim's argument is not watertight: it assumes all families have internet access.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Literally "not letting water in". American English often says "airtight".

entries.definition: used so often that it is no longer interesting or meaningful
entries.example_academic: The conclusion repeats a trite message about hard work.
entries.example_spoken: It sounds trite, but money really doesn't buy happiness.
entries.example_interview: It may sound trite, but my grandmother taught me the value of patience.
entries.example_discussion: Saying that "education is the key" is trite unless we explain which kind of education.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "It sounds trite, but…" is a natural way to introduce a simple truth.

entries.definition: used so often that it has lost its effect
entries.example_academic: The film relies on hackneyed images of small-town life.
entries.example_spoken: That's such a hackneyed line.
entries.example_interview: In my cover letter, I tried to avoid hackneyed phrases like "team player".
entries.example_discussion: The argument that technology isolates people has become hackneyed; we need fresher evidence.
entries.usage_note: Formal. Close to "trite" and "clichéd"; common in reviews of films and writing. Pronounced /ˈhækniːd/, two syllables.

entries.definition: not making you believe that something is true or good
entries.example_academic: The authors offer an unconvincing explanation for the drop in sales.
entries.example_spoken: His excuse was pretty unconvincing.
entries.example_interview: My first presentation was unconvincing because I read from my notes.
entries.example_discussion: I find Daniel's argument unconvincing, since it relies on a single example.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. A polite way to disagree. Not "inconvincing", which does not exist.

entries.definition: more important than anything else
entries.example_academic: Patient safety is paramount in any clinical trial.
entries.example_spoken: For me, family is paramount.
entries.example_interview: When choosing a job, work-life balance is paramount for me.
entries.example_discussion: Safety should be paramount, so I support Mia's call for stricter rules.
entries.usage_note: Formal. "Of paramount importance" is common. Not used before "more" or "most" (it is already absolute).

entries.definition: using too much force or authority, without care for people's feelings
entries.example_academic: The heavy-handed response of the police provoked further protests.
entries.example_spoken: The new rules feel a bit heavy-handed.
entries.example_interview: My first manager was quite heavy-handed, so I learned what kind of leader I don't want to be.
entries.example_discussion: Fining students for being late seems heavy-handed; a warning would be enough.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Criticizes a method rather than a goal. Not literally about heavy hands.

entries.definition: easy to understand or decide; not doubtful
entries.example_academic: The evidence is not as clear-cut as the headlines suggest.
entries.example_spoken: It's not a clear-cut choice.
entries.example_interview: Choosing my major wasn't clear-cut; I hesitated between biology and economics.
entries.example_discussion: The professor's question has no clear-cut answer, which is why the debate is useful.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Often negative: "not clear-cut", "far from clear-cut".

entries.definition: without a fixed limit, answer or end
entries.example_academic: Open-ended questions produced richer answers than multiple-choice items.
entries.example_spoken: The project is pretty open-ended.
entries.example_interview: I enjoy open-ended projects where I can decide the direction myself.
entries.example_discussion: An open-ended survey, as Lena suggests, would capture views the current form misses.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. "Open-ended question" = one with no fixed answer. Not "opened-ended".

entries.definition: having existed for a long time
entries.example_academic: The agreement ended a long-standing dispute over water rights.
entries.example_spoken: We have a long-standing tradition of Sunday lunch.
entries.example_interview: I have a long-standing interest in languages; I started Spanish at nine.
entries.example_discussion: Housing costs are a long-standing problem that no single policy will fix.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Hyphenated before a noun. Not "long-lasting", which describes duration into the future.

entries.definition: to fall very quickly and suddenly in amount or value
entries.example_academic: Share prices plummeted after the announcement.
entries.example_spoken: My grades plummeted when I started working nights.
entries.example_interview: My motivation plummeted in my second year, until I found a study group.
entries.example_discussion: Bird populations plummeted after the wetland was drained, which supports Lena's point.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Stronger than "fall" or "drop". Spelling: plummeted, plummeting (no double t).

entries.definition: to rise very quickly to a high level
entries.example_academic: Demand for electric cars soared last year.
entries.example_spoken: Rents have soared in my city.
entries.example_interview: When my blog was shared online, my number of readers soared overnight.
entries.example_discussion: Housing costs have soared, so Kim's idea of student cooperatives makes sense.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also used for birds and planes flying high. Opposite: "plummet".

entries.definition: to increase suddenly and strongly
entries.example_academic: Online sales surged during the holidays.
entries.example_spoken: Traffic to the site surged after the video.
entries.example_interview: Applications to my program surged after it appeared in the rankings.
entries.example_discussion: Bike use surged when the city added lanes, so more lanes seem worth the cost.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Common as a noun too: "a surge in demand". Suggests sudden energy.

entries.definition: to become gradually smaller in number or amount
entries.example_academic: The island's population dwindled over the century.
entries.example_spoken: My savings are dwindling fast.
entries.example_interview: My savings dwindled quickly during my first month in London.
entries.example_discussion: Volunteer numbers are dwindling, which is why Mia's idea of course credit is attractive.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Gradual decrease, often worrying. "Dwindling resources/numbers/support".

entries.definition: to stop growing or changing and stay at a low level
entries.example_academic: Sales flatlined for most of the year.
entries.example_spoken: My progress in French has kind of flatlined.
entries.example_interview: My running times flatlined for months, so I changed my training plan.
entries.example_discussion: Membership flatlined after the fee increase, which is strong evidence against raising it again.
entries.usage_note: Informal. Originally medical (no heartbeat on a monitor). Stronger and more negative than "level off".

entries.definition: to become gradually smaller or less until it stops
entries.example_academic: Infections tapered off as the summer went on.
entries.example_spoken: The rain finally tapered off.
entries.example_interview: My nerves tapered off after the first few minutes of the presentation.
entries.example_discussion: Interest in the app tapered off after a month, so the launch numbers are misleading.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Gradual, gentle decrease towards zero. Also used for doses of medicine.

entries.definition: to stop rising or falling and stay at the same level
entries.example_academic: Inflation is expected to level off next year.
entries.example_spoken: Prices seem to have leveled off.
entries.example_interview: My weight leveled off once I started cooking for myself.
entries.example_discussion: Enrollment rose for a decade and then leveled off, so new buildings may not be needed.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Spelling: leveled (US) / levelled (UK). Also "level out". Typical in graph descriptions.

entries.definition: to reach the lowest point before starting to rise again
entries.translation_fr: toucher le fond, atteindre son plus bas niveau
entries.example_academic: Analysts believe the housing market has bottomed out.
entries.example_spoken: I think my mood bottomed out in February.
entries.example_interview: My confidence bottomed out after a bad exam, but it slowly came back.
entries.example_discussion: Ticket sales seem to have bottomed out, so cutting the service now would be premature.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Implies recovery will follow. Common in economic news.

entries.definition: to rise suddenly and sharply, usually for a short time
entries.example_academic: Electricity use spikes on hot afternoons.
entries.example_spoken: My heart rate spiked during the interview.
entries.example_interview: My phone bill spiked when I used data abroad without checking.
entries.example_discussion: Accidents spike in the first week of winter, which supports Daniel's call for warnings.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. A short, sharp peak on a graph. Noun: "a spike in demand".

entries.definition: to increase slowly and by small amounts
entries.example_academic: Unemployment edged up to five percent.
entries.example_spoken: My scores have been edging up.
entries.example_interview: My savings edged up each month once I stopped eating out.
entries.example_discussion: Prices edged up only slightly, so Kim's fears of a crisis seem exaggerated.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Very small, gradual rise. Opposite: "edge down". Common in financial news.

entries.definition: to increase slightly
entries.example_academic: Consumer confidence ticked up in March.
entries.example_spoken: Attendance ticked up a bit after the new schedule.
entries.example_interview: My running speed ticked up after I joined a club.
entries.example_discussion: Turnout ticked up after online voting was introduced, as Jonah notes.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Small rise. Noun: "an uptick in". Opposite: "tick down".

entries.definition: to reduce something to half its previous size or amount
entries.example_academic: The new process halved production time.
entries.example_spoken: We halved the recipe because we were only two.
entries.example_interview: Cycling to campus halved my travel costs.
entries.example_discussion: Shorter lectures would not halve learning, but they might halve boredom.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Pronounced /hæv/ in US English, /hɑːv/ in British English. Opposite: "double". Not "half" (the noun).

entries.definition: to be more numerous than another group
entries.translation_fr: être plus nombreux que, dépasser en nombre
entries.example_academic: Women now outnumber men in medical schools.
entries.example_spoken: In my class, the international students outnumbered us.
entries.example_interview: In my engineering class, men outnumbered women three to one.
entries.example_discussion: Cars still outnumber bikes on campus, so better lanes alone may not change habits.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Subject is the larger group. "Outnumber by two to one" is a common pattern.

entries.definition: to fall suddenly and by a large amount, often staying low
entries.example_academic: Car sales slumped during the recession.
entries.example_spoken: Our team slumped in the second half of the season.
entries.example_interview: My energy slumps every afternoon around three, so I schedule easy tasks then.
entries.example_discussion: Bookshop sales slumped when prices rose, which confirms Mia's point about demand.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Also a noun: "an economic slump". Suggests a long, weak period after the fall.

entries.definition: to rise extremely quickly to a very high level
entries.example_academic: The cost of insulin skyrocketed over the decade.
entries.example_spoken: Our rent just skyrocketed this year.
entries.example_interview: My phone bill skyrocketed when I forgot to turn off roaming.
entries.example_discussion: Tuition has skyrocketed since the 1980s, so free courses deserve serious discussion.
entries.usage_note: Informal to neutral. Even stronger than "soar". In formal writing, "rose sharply" may be safer.

entries.definition: to go down slightly, usually for a short time
entries.example_academic: Temperatures dipped below freezing overnight.
entries.example_spoken: My grades dipped a bit last term.
entries.example_interview: My motivation always dips in November, when the days get shorter.
entries.example_discussion: Library visits dipped during the renovation, but they should recover, as Lena says.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Small, temporary fall. Noun: "a dip in sales". Doubling: dipped, dipping.

entries.definition: a fall in business or economic activity
entries.example_academic: The downturn hit the construction sector hardest.
entries.example_spoken: My parents' shop struggled during the downturn.
entries.example_interview: My first job offer was canceled because of the economic downturn.
entries.example_discussion: During a downturn, cutting training budgets is tempting but short-sighted.
entries.usage_note: Neutral. Mostly economic. Opposite: "upturn". Softer than "recession", which has a technical meaning.

entries.definition: to fall suddenly and steeply in value or level
entries.example_academic: The currency nosedived after the election.
entries.example_spoken: My confidence nosedived after that comment.
entries.example_interview: My grades took a nosedive when I worked thirty hours a week.
entries.example_discussion: Ridership nosedived when fares rose, a clear warning against Daniel's proposal.
entries.usage_note: Informal. From planes diving nose first. "Take a nosedive" is the most common pattern.
